name: Common VAT system Directive
impact_assessment: none for the 2006 recast; SWD(2016) 379 (e-commerce); SWD(2022) 393 (digital age)
evidence_rating: moderate for VAT in general, thin for the Directive's digital rules: Commission forecasts and collection data, one strong causal study on VAT incidence
summary: The VAT Directive sets the EU's common VAT rules, which have been updated for online sales. Since the 2021 e-commerce reform, VAT collected through the EU's one-stop-shop rose to EUR 33 billion in 2024, though this is gross collection rather than a measured net gain. Independent research using EU VAT changes shows price rises from VAT increases are passed on about twice as fully as VAT cuts; the 2025 digital VAT reform is forecast to raise EUR 135-177 billion over ten years.

indicators.objective: The 2004 proposal was a recast of the Sixth VAT Directive with no indicators; evidence concerns later digital amendments (e-services 2015, e-commerce package 2021, VAT in the Digital Age 2025)

indicators.indicator: Extend one-stop shop, abolish EUR 22 import exemption
indicators.target_or_baseline: Status quo losses EUR 7bn/yr by 2020; preferred option cuts business VAT admin burden 42% (EUR 1.8bn)
indicators.evidence: OSS/IOSS VAT declared rose from EUR 26.3bn (2023) to EUR 33.1bn (2024), about EUR 88bn in 2021-2024; MOSS for e-services collected about EUR 3bn in 2015 and saved firms ~EUR 500m. Revenue is gross collection through the schemes, not a net causal effect.

indicators.indicator: Digital reporting, platform deemed supplier, single registration
indicators.target_or_baseline: Net impact EUR 172-214bn 2023-2032; extra VAT EUR 135-177bn; business savings EUR 50.6bn
indicators.evidence: Adopted 2025; phased in to 2035; not yet measured.

indicators.objective: Pass-through of VAT to consumer prices
indicators.evidence: Using EU VAT changes 1996-2015, prices respond about twice as much to VAT increases as to decreases.

literature.citation: European Commission (2016), Impact assessment on modernising VAT for cross-border B2C e-commerce, SWD(2016) 379
literature.title: Impact assessment on modernising VAT for cross-border B2C e-commerce
literature.headline: MOSS (2015): ~EUR 3bn VAT paid, ~70% of e-service supplies, saved businesses ~EUR 500m; status quo: cross-border compliance costs EUR 4.2bn a year, VAT losses EUR 7bn a year by 2020; preferred option cuts admin burden 42% (EUR 1.8bn)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected its e-commerce VAT reform to cut business paperwork by 42% and close a EUR 7 billion a year revenue gap.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Report on the application of the VAT e-commerce package for 2024, VAT One Stop Shop portal, 14 July 2025
literature.title: Report on the application of the VAT e-commerce package for 2024
literature.venue: VAT One Stop Shop portal, 14 July 2025
literature.headline: VAT declared via the three OSS schemes rose from EUR 26.3bn in 2023 to EUR 33.1bn in 2024 (+26%); about EUR 88bn declared 2021-2024
literature.summary_plain: VAT collected through the EU's one-stop-shop for online sales reached EUR 33 billion in 2024, up 26% on 2023.
literature.quality: gross collections; not a causal estimate

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact assessment on VAT in the digital age (executive summary SWD(2022) 394), SWD(2022) 393
literature.title: Impact assessment on VAT in the digital age (executive summary SWD(2022) 394)
literature.headline: Preferred approach: EUR 172-214bn net impact 2023-2032; EUR 50.6bn savings; EUR 135-177bn additional VAT revenue; EUR 11.3bn new reporting costs for business; 280,000 SMEs benefit from extended OSS
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected digitising VAT to raise EUR 135-177 billion of extra VAT and save firms about EUR 50 billion over ten years.

literature.citation: Benzarti, Carloni, Harju & Kosonen (2020), What Goes Up May Not Come Down: Asymmetric Incidence of Value-Added Taxes, Journal of Political Economy 128(12) (NBER WP 23849)
literature.title: What Goes Up May Not Come Down: Asymmetric Incidence of Value-Added Taxes
literature.method: quasi-experimental (two exogenous VAT changes) plus panel of all EU VAT changes 1996-2015
literature.headline: Prices respond twice as much to VAT increases as to decreases; asymmetry raises profits and markups and persists for years; similar asymmetry across all EU VAT changes 1996-2015
literature.summary_plain: Studying VAT changes across the EU, economists found shops pass on VAT rises about twice as fully as VAT cuts.
literature.quality: strong causal design; about VAT rates, not the Directive itself
